prompt:
Two people transcribed the SAME table, the Schedule of Activities of one clinical-trial protocol. The REFERENCE transcription is taken as correct. Below are the row labels each of them wrote down. You do two things: (1) pair each REFERENCE label with the CANDIDATE label that is the same row of the source table, and (2) grade how well each paired CANDIDATE label reproduces the content of its REFERENCE label.

Each label names one ROW of the table: an activity, assessment or procedure (for example "Informed consent", "Vital signs", "12-lead ECG").

STEP 1 - ALIGN
For every REFERENCE label find the CANDIDATE label that is the transcription of the same row of the source table: the same physical row, at the same place in the table.
- Both lists are in table order. Order is a strong cue: use it together with the text.
- A CANDIDATE that is evidently the transcription of a given REFERENCE row is its counterpart even if its text has mistakes or leaves something out; the mistakes are graded in step 2. A section heading and an item under it are different rows. If a CANDIDATE merges several REFERENCE rows into one, or splits one into several, pair only the closest and give null for the rest.
- Use null only when the CANDIDATE list has no counterpart for that REFERENCE row (it was skipped, or merged into another). Do not use null merely because the text differs or because you would grade it wrong.
- One-to-one: a CANDIDATE label may be used at most once. Do not assume the lists have the same length: either side may have extra rows.
- Ids carry no meaning.

STEP 2 - CHECK EACH PAIR
Compare the paired CANDIDATE text with the REFERENCE text and answer two yes/no questions (true/false).
"content": do the two texts differ in ANY character? Ignore only whitespace (spaces, line breaks). Differences of form count here and only here:
- case, punctuation, trademark signs;
- a footnote marker written as a superscript, as a plain trailing letter or digit, glued to the word or separate ("Spirometry b" / "Spirometryᵇ" / "Spirometryb");
- an abbreviation every reader expands the same way ("MRI" / "Magnetic resonance imaging"; "BMI" / "Body mass index");
- an obvious spelling or OCR slip that leaves the activity unmistakable.
"semantic": does the CANDIDATE label mean something different from the REFERENCE label, or leave out information the REFERENCE states, so that a reader would interpret the row differently or know less about it? This covers a contradiction (typically the CANDIDATE names a different activity, specimen, instrument, dose, number or unit ("Left knee X-ray" -> "Right knee X-ray"; "Systolic pressure" -> "Diastolic pressure"; "Dose 1" -> "Dose 2"; "Biopsy" -> "Bone scan")) and an omission (typically part of the activity name or a qualifier in the REFERENCE is left out ("Spirometry/ peak flow" -> "Spirometry"; "Questionnaires (A and B)" -> "Questionnaires (A)"; "12-lead ECG (triplicate)" -> "12-lead ECG")). Differences of form are not semantic. A dropped or shortened header-row NAME whose value is kept is not semantic.
Rules:
- "semantic" true implies "content" true.
- Footnote markers (a short letter, number or symbol attached to a label that points to a footnote): a marker that is DIFFERENT from the one in the REFERENCE, or a marker on a label whose REFERENCE has none, is semantic, because it points the reader to the wrong footnote. The same marker written in another form (superscript, attached or spaced), or a marker the CANDIDATE leaves out, is "content" only.
- Extra information in the CANDIDATE that the REFERENCE does not have, and that does not contradict it, is "content" only (footnote markers excepted, see above).
- Judge only what the two texts say. Do not guess what the source table contained.
